newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's next premier shuns golf, scandal.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's next premier shuns golf, scandal.

text.p: He spurns golf and fancy restaurants, but the man picked as South Korea's next prime minister is most famous for steering clear of scandal and corruption.
That virtue cost Koh Kun, 59, his job as mayor of Seoul in 1990 but probably secured his nomination on Tuesday as the country's new premier, political analysts said.

Koh quit as mayor in 1990 rather than bow to the administration of then head of state Roh Tae-woo, which political analysts said tried to strong-arm him into a dubious multi-million dollar property deal with the Hanbo Group, the country's 14th largest conglomerate.
Now his job will be to help rescue President Kim Young-sam from a fresh financial scandal involving Hanbo during a presidential election year.
In a lengthy career in government that spanned the notoriously corrupt administrations of Roh and his predecessor Chun Doo Hwan, Koh has never been tainted by dirty money.

"Koh has spent such a long time in public office, yet has never been involved in a corruption scandal," said Ra Jong-yil, a political science professor at Kyunghee University who has known Koh since their student days.
"He doesn't play golf because he believes it's a luxurious sport that's often associated with corruption."
Friends and associates of Koh describe an outgoing character who prefers plain local eateries to expensive hotel restaurants.
Roh and Chun are both serving long jail sentences after being convicted of bribery and other abuses while in office.
But the man responsible for hounding them through the courts -- current president Kim -- has seen his reputation as an anti-graft crusader dragged through the mud by the latest Hanbo crisis.
Three of Kim's closest aides are in custody on charges of influence peddling to secure loans to bankrupt Hanbo Steel Co that eventually mounted to $5.8 billion.

"President Kim's camp needed someone clean to overcome the public disappointment over failed reform and endless scandals," said Ra, who is also a member of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo was found guilty in 1991 of bribing officials to try to secure rights to build thousands of apartments in a Seoul suburb. He was jailed for six months.

Political analysts said Koh, mayor of Seoul from 1988 to 1990, stepped down in protest at pressure he felt was coming from the central government to bend re-zoning rules and approve the housing complex.
Chung was arrested again in the latest scandal on charges of bribery and embezzlement involving loans to Hanbo Steel.
Koh held cabinet portfolios for home affairs, transportation, and agriculture and fisheries during Chun's 1980-88 administration. He has been president of Myongji University since 1994.
"Koh Kun is an excellent choice for President Kim because of his strong administrative ability," said Cho Chang-hyun, a political science professor at Hanyang University.

Koh's family roots in economically-backward Cholla province had made him an unlikely candidate for high office in a country of regional enmities where power is monopolised by residents of wealthy Kyongsang province.
Resentment among Cholla natives at their privileged next door neighour have driven them into the arms of the political opposition.
Koh was governor of South Cholla province in 1975-79.
Among Myongji University students, he is popular for his open-mindedness and a personal touch.
"Koh tried to get to know us better. He is not an authoritarian like other college presidents. He really listens to us," said a member of the student body.
